title: The Orchard Core Data Pipelines module

chapters.title: The Orchard Core Data Pipelines module
chapters.subtitle: Read, transform and deliver the data of your site

steps.text: Sites hold data that people need elsewhere: a list for finance, a file for a partner, rows to bring in. The Data Pipelines module reads data, changes it and delivers it, without code. In this video, we'll build and run a first pipeline.

Data often has to leave the site or enter it: a spreadsheet of content items, a nightly file for another system, or a CSV file whose rows become content items. Done by hand, the work repeats every time.
The Data Pipelines module lets an administrator design this work as a pipeline: a set of connected steps. Sources read rows from the data of the site. Transforms change the rows.
Files write the rows to a CSV file, an Excel workbook, or another format. Destinations deliver the result: to the media library, by email, to a server, or as content items.

chapters.title: Enable Data Pipelines
chapters.subtitle: A feature, and two pages in the Tools menu

steps.text: Data Pipelines is a feature of the site. Let's open Tools, Features, and search for it.

Enabling Data Pipelines also enables Data Pipelines Core, which provides the data sources and the file formats. The Tools menu then has a Data Pipelines section, with two pages: Pipelines, and Run History.
The Pipelines page lists the pipelines of the site, and it is empty. Add Pipeline opens the form for the first one.
A pipeline needs a name. Let's type Blog posts, and select Create. The designer opens next.

The designer has Steps on the left, grouped as Sources, Transforms, Files and Destinations. The canvas is empty and offers to start with a source. On the right, a panel has the Pipeline, Issues and History tabs.

chapters.title: Build a pipeline
chapters.subtitle: A source, a file and a destination

steps.text: A pipeline starts with a source. Add a data source opens the data sets you may read: the content items of each content type, the users, and the results of saved queries.
Let's add the Blog Post content items. A Read a data source step appears on the canvas, and its settings open: the fields to read, filters, and a maximum number of rows.
In the Data tab, Preview runs the pipeline up to this step, on a sample of the rows. The Fields tab lists the fields the step produces.
To add the next step, click the output port on the right edge of the step. The list offers the steps that can receive rows. Let's choose Create a file.
Create a file writes the rows to a file. Its settings hold the format, which is CSV by default, and the file name, without its extension. Let's name the file blog-posts.
A file has to go somewhere. Click the output port of Create a file, and choose Save to the media library. Its settings name a folder, and whether to replace a file with the same name.
The designer saves the draft as you work. The Issues tab lists what must be fixed before publishing. Publish creates the first version, which is the one runs use.
Run starts the published version. The run is queued and executes in the background, with the access of the user who published the pipeline.
The History tab lists the runs. With a run selected, each step on the canvas shows its status, and the number of rows or files it handled.
Open the run shows its page: each step with its status and its rows in and out, what the run delivered, and its log. Here, it saved a CSV file to the media library.
The Run History page lists the runs, the most recent first, with their status, version, duration, and who started them. A link shows the runs of every pipeline.
On the Pipelines page, the pipeline shows its version and the status of its last run. Its Actions menu can run it again, open its Run history, or delete it.

Pipelines do more than this first export: transforms filter, sort, group, join and calculate, and destinations include download links, email, FTP and SFTP servers, and web APIs. Some steps need another feature enabled. A workflow can run a pipeline on a schedule.

Three permissions control pipelines: Manage data pipelines, Run data pipelines, and View data pipelines and their runs. The Administrator role has all three. Manage data pipelines is security critical, since a published pipeline runs with the access of its publisher.

steps.text: Data Pipelines reads the data of your site, changes it and delivers it, and keeps a history of its runs. Thanks for watching.
